questions.stem: A text's 'context of production' refers to:
options: the time and place in which the events of the story are set
the order in which the text presents its events to the reader
the historical, social and cultural conditions in which it was written
the circumstances and values of the readers who encounter the text today
questions.explanation: The context of production surrounds the writer and the act of writing. The circumstances of today's readers make up the context of reception, the term most often confused with it.

questions.stem: A novel written in 1950s Britain is set in ancient Rome. Which statement is accurate?
options: Its setting and its context of production are both ancient Rome, so 1950s Britain is irrelevant to its meaning.
Its context of production is the present day, because that is when readers are encountering it.
Its setting is 1950s Britain, because a novel is always set in the place where it was written.
Its setting is ancient Rome, but its context of production is 1950s Britain, which may shape its concerns.
questions.explanation: Setting is the world inside the story, while context of production is the world in which the author wrote. A novel about the past can still reflect the anxieties and values of its own time, which is why the distinction matters.

questions.stem: A novel written in 2010 depicts convict-era Van Diemen's Land. Its representation of the convict era is most likely shaped by:
options: only the values held by convicts and officials of the colonial era
nothing outside the text, because historical fiction is purely factual
only the personal experiences of the convicts' living descendants
the values of the early 21st century as well as the past it depicts
questions.explanation: Historical fiction looks at the past through the concerns of its own present, so a recent novel may question colonial attitudes that writers of the period took for granted. It is a constructed representation, not a neutral record of facts.

questions.stem: Which statement best reflects the idea that context is 'inscribed' in a text?
options: Details such as diction, settings and assumptions about characters carry traces of the culture that produced the text.
Context can be found only in biographies of the author, so it must be researched entirely outside the text itself.
A text's context is whatever the reader brings to it, so the text itself contains no traces of its time.
Context is inscribed only when the author names a date and place explicitly at the start of the text.
questions.explanation: Contextual meaning is present in the text's own language, values and representations, which close reading can uncover. Outside research can help, but the evidence of context is already in the words on the page.

questions.stem: 'Mr Hale worked his labourers sixteen hours a day, and was much admired at church for his thrift.' The juxtaposition in this sentence most likely:
options: endorses Mr Hale's thrift as a model of Christian virtue
shows that the narrator shares the congregation's admiration
presents the labourers' long hours as a fair, normal arrangement
critiques the hypocrisy of a society that admires exploitation
questions.explanation: Placing brutal working hours beside public praise for 'thrift' invites readers to see the gap between the community's piety and its practice. The irony is in the narration, so the narrator is exposing the admiration rather than sharing it.

questions.stem: Austen's Pride and Prejudice opens: 'It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.' The irony of this sentence most likely:
options: mocks a society preoccupied with securing wealthy husbands for its daughters
states the narrator's sincere belief that every rich man is seeking a wife
celebrates the freedom of wealthy single men from the burden of marriage
criticises the factory conditions brought about by the Industrial Revolution
questions.explanation: The 'universal truth' is really the wish of families seeking rich husbands for their daughters, so the grand claim gently satirises a social obsession with marriage and money. Reading the sentence as sincere misses its ironic inversion of who wants what.

questions.stem: In a novel, a young woman who mocks the class system is punished for it, then repents; the narrator approves of her change. This suggests the text ultimately:
options: presents no view of its own about the class system that it describes
rejects the narrator's approval as the opinion of a fool
endorses the class hierarchy that it first appeared to question
critiques the class system consistently from beginning to end
questions.explanation: Endings and narrative judgement are strong guides to a text's values: punishing the rebel and approving her repentance restores the hierarchy. A text can raise a challenge to a value only in order to defeat it.

questions.stem: A first-person narrator boasts about his harsh treatment of his servants, and the novel shows their suffering in detail. Readers are most likely meant to:
options: ignore the servants, because the narrator gives them no importance
judge the narrator, as the novel critiques the attitudes he holds
accept the narrator's views, because a narrator speaks for the author
admire the narrator, since he is honest about how he treats others
questions.explanation: A narrator is not the author, and the novel's detailed attention to the servants' suffering works against his boasting. The gap between what he says and what readers see is how the text signals its critique.

questions.stem: A Victorian narrator remarks: 'Of course, no respectable lady would walk unaccompanied to the station.' The phrase 'of course' signals:
options: the narrator's open criticism of the custom described
a sudden shift from third-person to second-person narration
an anachronism that sets the novel in the present
a social norm the narrator assumes readers share
questions.explanation: 'Of course' treats the rule as obvious, revealing an assumption of the time about women's freedom of movement. Nothing in the sentence questions the custom; it is presented as common sense.

questions.stem: In Juliet's line 'O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?', the word 'wherefore' means:
options: whereas
wherever
why
where
questions.explanation: 'Wherefore' meant 'for what reason', so Juliet is asking why he must be a Montague, not where he is. The mistaken modern reading as 'where' is a classic example of a word whose meaning has shifted.

questions.stem: In older English texts, 'awful' often meant:
options: full of fear and dread
lacking proper manners
inspiring awe or reverence
extremely bad or unpleasant
questions.explanation: 'Awful' first described something worthy of awe, such as the majesty of God; its everyday meaning of 'very bad' developed later. Reading the older sense as 'very bad' can reverse a passage's meaning entirely.

questions.stem: In a novel published in the 1920s, a guest at a party is described as 'gay'. In this context the word most likely means:
options: late and in a hurry
quiet and shy
cheerful and lively
unwell and pale
questions.explanation: Until the mid-20th century, 'gay' commonly meant light-hearted or merry. Knowing how words have shifted in meaning prevents readers from imposing a modern sense on an older text.

questions.stem: In Elizabethan drama, a servant who suddenly addresses his master as 'thou' instead of 'you' is most likely signalling:
options: deeper respect, since 'thou' was the most formal pronoun
a change of scene from the court to the countryside
that the master has been promoted to a higher rank
disrespect, by breaking the expected forms of address
questions.explanation: In Elizabethan English, 'you' was the polite form owed to superiors, while 'thou' was used to intimates and inferiors, so a servant using it to a master could be insolent. The tempting error is to assume archaic 'thou' must be the more formal word.

questions.stem: A modern reader assumes that every word in a 17th-century poem carries its current meaning. The main risk is:
options: understanding the poem too literally and too accurately
confusing the poem's rhyme scheme with its metre
treating the poem's speaker as its author
misreading words whose meanings have shifted over time
questions.explanation: Words carry historical import, and many, such as 'nice', 'silly' and 'awful', have changed meaning over centuries. Treating the speaker as the author is a separate error that has nothing to do with the age of the words.

questions.stem: In a 19th-century travel narrative, an inhabited land is described as 'empty' and 'waiting to be tamed'. Read in context, this language most likely:
options: reflects colonial assumptions used to justify taking land already occupied
records accurately that no people at all were living on the land at that time
expresses an ecological concern to protect the land from development
shows the narrator's deep respect for the land's existing inhabitants
questions.explanation: Calling occupied land 'empty' erases its inhabitants and frames possession as a natural act of improvement, a key colonial idea. The words reveal the coloniser's viewpoint rather than the reality of the place.

questions.stem: A story of the 1890s celebrates life on an outback station but never mentions the Aboriginal people whose Country it is set on. A contextual reading might argue that this absence:
options: means the story has nothing to say about the colonial context of its own time
reflects a settler perspective that erased Aboriginal presence from the landscape
shows that Aboriginal people had no connection to the land where the story is set
proves that the author was writing a work of fantasy rather than about real places
questions.explanation: Silences in a text are also shaped by context: leaving out the Traditional Owners reflects and reinforces a colonial view of the land as settler territory. The absence says something about the text's viewpoint, not about who was actually there.

questions.stem: The heroic couplet's balanced, closed pairs of rhymed lines dominated much 18th-century (Augustan) English poetry. In context, the form is often linked to the period's value of:
options: fragmentation and doubt
the supernatural and terror
reason, order and balance
emotion and spontaneity
questions.explanation: The neat symmetry of the heroic couplet suited an age that prized reason, wit and classical order. Emotion and spontaneity were the values of the Romantic poets who reacted against Augustan restraint.

questions.stem: In 'Dulce et Decorum Est', written during the First World War, Wilfred Owen calls the Latin motto 'it is sweet and fitting to die for one's country' 'The old Lie'. In context, the poem:
options: counters patriotic rhetoric that glorified dying for one's country
celebrates soldiers' sacrifice in the spirit of the Latin motto
was written long after the war as a calm historical reflection on it
addresses the enemy soldiers who carried out the gas attack
questions.explanation: Owen, a serving officer, sets the horror of a gas attack against the noble language of recruitment and propaganda, exposing it as a lie. He wrote the poem during the war, which gives its witness and anger their force.

questions.stem: The bush ballads published in The Bulletin in the 1890s often celebrated:
options: mateship, the bush and the itinerant bush worker as distinctly Australian
the refinement of Sydney society and its careful imitation of English manners
the city as a place of opportunity, comfort and fulfilling work
a strict class hierarchy modelled closely on English rural life
questions.explanation: Writers such as Banjo Paterson and Henry Lawson helped shape a national legend around the bush, mateship and the drover and shearer, in the decade before Federation. These ballads more often set the bush against the city than praised urban life.

questions.stem: A novel set during the Great Depression opens with an epigraph from a 1930s newspaper. The epigraph most likely:
options: shows that the novel was written by a journalist of that decade
situates the narrative in its historical moment and frames its concerns
reveals the ending of the novel before the narrative has even begun
establishes the novel as an epistolary text told through newspaper reports
questions.explanation: An epigraph is a quotation placed at the start of a text to set up its themes and, here, to anchor the story in its period. One quotation does not make a novel epistolary or reveal who wrote it.

questions.stem: In a novel set in 1850, a character checks the time on a digital watch. This is an:
options: allusion
analepsis
allegorical device
anachronism
questions.explanation: An anachronism places something outside its proper time, and here the watch is more than a century too early. Writers sometimes use anachronism deliberately to link the past with the present.

questions.stem: The level of formality of the language in a text or a character's speech is its:
options: motif
register
metre
syntax
questions.explanation: Register ranges from formal to colloquial and often signals social class, situation or period. Syntax is the arrangement of words in sentences, which can contribute to register but is not the same thing.

questions.stem: A novel renders a working-class character's speech in phonetic dialect, while the narrator and middle-class characters use standard English. A contextual reading might note that this choice:
options: removes all social meaning, since dialect is simply a record of how people sound
places the novel in the present day, because dialect writing is a modern technique
can reinforce class hierarchy by marking the working-class character as different
shows that the working-class character is the novel's narrator and its moral centre
questions.explanation: Representing only some characters' speech as 'non-standard' sets the narrator's language as the norm and the dialect speaker as other, which can carry class assumptions. Dialect writing is long established, and it is never a neutral recording.

questions.stem: On the Elizabethan public stage, female roles were played by:
options: masked chorus members
the playwright
boy actors
adult actresses
questions.explanation: Women did not act on the English public stage until after the Restoration in 1660, so boys played female parts. Knowing this adds layers to plays in which female characters disguise themselves as men.

questions.stem: A play written for an Elizabethan audience shows the murder of a king followed by unnatural storms. In context, the storms most likely reflect the belief that:
options: the natural world is indifferent to the fate of human rulers
disrupting the divinely ordained order brings disorder to nature itself
storms are random events with no link at all to human affairs or politics
kings were elected by the people and could be removed at will
questions.explanation: Many Elizabethans understood the world through the Great Chain of Being, a hierarchy in which the king's place was ordained by God, so killing him disturbed the whole cosmos. Reading the storms as mere weather misses this context.

questions.stem: In Victorian 'separate spheres' ideology, men and women were assigned to:
options: public life and work for men, the domestic home for women
the domestic home for men, public life and work for women
equal shares of public and domestic responsibility
the city for men and the countryside for women
questions.explanation: The ideology placed men in the world of work, politics and commerce and confined women to the home as moral guardians of family life. Many Victorian novels dramatise women pressing against these limits.

questions.stem: The phrase 'the angel in the house', from a popular Victorian poem by Coventry Patmore, came to stand for:
options: a servant who managed a large household for her employers
the ideal of the selfless, devoted wife confined to the home
a woman who rejected marriage in order to pursue a career in writing
a ghost haunting the domestic interiors of Gothic novels
questions.explanation: Patmore's poem idealised a wife's self-sacrifice and domestic devotion, and the phrase became shorthand for that Victorian ideal. Virginia Woolf later wrote that a woman writer had to 'kill' the angel in the house in order to write freely.

questions.stem: Fiction of the 1890s featuring the 'New Woman' typically presented heroines who:
options: lived in a future society in which gender roles no longer existed
were punished by the narrative for any interest in domestic duty
sought education, work and independence beyond traditional marriage
found fulfilment by returning to a quiet and dutiful domestic life
questions.explanation: The New Woman was a figure of debate in the late 19th century, representing women who challenged conventional roles in education, work, dress and marriage. Texts featuring her register the social controversies of that context.

questions.stem: Victorian novels often have the 'fallen woman', a woman who has broken sexual codes, die or be exiled by the end. This convention most often reflected:
options: a medical theory that such women were especially prone to illness
the harsh moral judgement society placed on women who transgressed
a belief that men and women were held to identical moral standards
the authors' wish to show such women rewarded for their courage
questions.explanation: The fallen woman's fate encoded a double standard: women were punished far more severely than men for the same transgressions. Some novels reproduce this judgement, while others use the convention to question it.

questions.stem: In the 19th century, Mary Ann Evans published as 'George Eliot', and the Brontë sisters first published as Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell. This context suggests that:
options: male pseudonyms were required by every publisher for every first novel
the authors wanted to write in a genre that was reserved for men
women writers faced prejudice that could affect how their work was received
women were legally forbidden from publishing any novels under their own names
questions.explanation: Writers adopted male or ambiguous names partly to be judged on their work rather than on assumptions about women's writing. No law forbade women from publishing under their own names; the pressure was social.

questions.stem: Virginia Woolf argued in A Room of One's Own that 'a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction'. A reader applying this to a text in context would consider:
options: how material conditions, such as income and privacy, shaped writing
how the setting of the text is limited to a single domestic room
how a novel's chapters should be divided into separate rooms
how money is the main theme of every novel written by a woman
questions.explanation: Woolf's point is that the material circumstances of women's lives, not lack of talent, limited their writing. Reading it as a claim about settings or themes misses its argument about the conditions of production.

questions.stem: A playwright living under strict censorship sets a play about a tyrant in ancient Rome. This choice of setting most likely allows the play to:
options: avoid any connection with the politics of the playwright's time
record the history of ancient Rome with complete accuracy
appeal only to an audience of scholars of the classical world
comment on present-day politics indirectly, at a safe distance
questions.explanation: Displacing a story in time or place lets writers explore dangerous ideas while maintaining deniability, and audiences can recognise the parallel. The historical setting is a strategy for commenting on the present, not a retreat from it.

questions.stem: Industrial or 'condition-of-England' novels of the 1840s and 1850s describe soot-blackened factory towns. These settings most often conveyed concern about:
options: the human costs of industrialisation for the working poor
the dangers of the wilderness beyond settled farmland
the decline of the monarchy's power over parliament
the spread of new communication technologies such as the internet
questions.explanation: These novels used the smoke and squalor of mill towns to draw middle-class readers' attention to the suffering of workers. The setting carries the social concern, rather than serving only as background.

questions.stem: In In Memoriam A.H.H. (1850), Tennyson writes of 'Nature, red in tooth and claw'. In context, the phrase most likely reflects:
options: an anxiety that a brutal, indifferent nature undermines faith in a loving God
a direct response to Darwin's On the Origin of Species and its argument
a Romantic confidence that nature reveals a benevolent and loving divine order
a celebration of hunting as a noble pastime of the English gentry
questions.explanation: Tennyson's poem, mourning his friend Arthur Hallam, wrestles with geological and scientific ideas that seemed to show nature as violent and careless of life. It was published nine years before Darwin's book of 1859, so it cannot be a response to it.

questions.stem: A comedy first staged in the 1590s mocks a foreign character in ways its original audience shared. A modern production presents him with sympathy. This shows that:
options: the original play must have intended him all along to be a sympathetic character
modern productions are not permitted to alter the tone of earlier plays
the play has lost all connection with the context in which it was written
changing contexts of reception can shift how a text's representations are read
questions.explanation: The words remain the same, but a later audience with different values responds differently, and productions can draw out that difference. Recognising the original hostility is part of reading the play in its context of production.

questions.stem: A Renaissance play shows daughters being 'given' in marriage by their fathers, with little say of their own. The feature of society this most clearly reflects is:
options: patriarchal authority over women's choices
the equal legal rights of women and men
the absence of any rules about marriage
the power of daughters over family property
questions.explanation: Fathers' control over daughters' marriages reflects a patriarchal society in which women passed from a father's authority to a husband's. Plays of the period often dramatise the conflict this creates.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'This 1890s novel proves that everyone in the 1890s believed women belonged at home.' The main weakness of this claim is that it:
options: treats one text's representation as proof of what everyone believed
names a whole decade instead of the year the novel was published
discusses the novel's values rather than only its literary features
uses the word 'novel' when the correct term would be 'text'
questions.explanation: A single text is one constructed representation that may endorse, question or exaggerate the views of its time, so it cannot prove what everyone thought. The 1890s also saw active debate about the New Woman, so 'everyone' is historically inaccurate as well.

questions.stem: Studying a text 'in its context' means examining how the text:
options: represents and responds to the time and culture that produced it
can be read without reference to any history beyond its own pages
follows the rules of its genre, regardless of when it was written
would be rewritten if it were produced today by a modern author
questions.explanation: Contextual study asks how a text reflects, endorses or critiques the ideas and concerns of its time and culture. Genre conventions matter too, but they are only one part of what context includes.

questions.stem: A text's 'context of reception' refers to:
options: the historical period in which the story's events take place
the genre conventions the text follows or deliberately breaks
the circumstances and values of the readers who encounter it
the conditions in which the author wrote and first published it
questions.explanation: Reception belongs to readers, and it changes as each new audience brings its own values to the text. The conditions in which the author wrote are the context of production.

questions.stem: A text is said to 'endorse' a value when it:
options: presents that value favourably, for example by rewarding the characters who hold it
mentions that value at least once in a character's dialogue or in the narration
punishes the characters who hold that value and shows them to be mistaken
leaves that value entirely unexamined and never shows any character acting on it
questions.explanation: Endorsement shows in how a text treats a value: through narrative approval, outcomes and the sympathy it builds. Merely mentioning a value is not endorsing it, since a text may raise a value only to critique it.

questions.stem: The 'Great Chain of Being', a worldview common in Elizabethan England, was:
options: a theory that all living things evolved gradually from simpler forms over vast periods of time
a political belief that every person was equal and that rulers should be chosen by the people
a literary convention requiring every play to be divided into five linked acts of equal length
a divinely ordained hierarchy running from God through angels, kings and people down to animals, plants and stones
questions.explanation: The Chain placed everything in a fixed order, so disrupting one link, such as by killing a king, threatened the whole. Evolutionary theory belongs to the 19th century and directly challenged such fixed hierarchies.
